widget.Oscillation.title: Neutrino oscillation: distance and energy
widget.Oscillation.view: Probability that a neutrino has changed flavour, as a function of distance divided by energy, with the current setting marked
widget.Oscillation.cap: Two-flavour approximation, round-number parameters. Where the oscillation is too fast to resolve, the curve shows its average.
widget.Oscillation.note: Two-flavour approximation: P = sin²2θ · sin²(1.27 Δm² L / E), with Δm² in eV², L in km and E in GeV. The real neutrinos mix three flavours, and matter in the Earth changes the picture slightly; both are left out here. Parameters are rounded.
widget.RingClassifier.title: Muon or electron? Read the ring
widget.RingClassifier.view: Simulated pattern of {n} lit light sensors on the tank wall, forming a ring
widget.RingClassifier.cap: Each dot is one light sensor that fired; bigger and darker means more light.
widget.RingClassifier.prompt: Pick one to see the edge-sharpness measurement.
widget.RingClassifier.stopping: (It stopped inside the tank, so the ring is also partly filled.)
widget.RingClassifier.metricSays: A cut on this number says
widget.RingClassifier.profView: Light collected at each distance from the ring centre, with the outer edge marked
widget.RingClassifier.note: Simulated rings. A muon flies straight, so its ring has a thin, sharp edge; an electron starts a small shower, whose many cones blur the edge. The metric is the distance over which the light density falls from 80 % to 20 % of its peak, divided by the ring radius; below about {cut} counts as sharp. Noisy events can fool both you and the cut.
widget.IbdCoincidence.title: Delayed coincidence: pairs in time
widget.IbdCoincidence.view: Six milliseconds of simulated flashes in the detector: energy of each flash against time; {n} accepted pairs are drawn as connected lines
widget.IbdCoincidence.cap: A 6 ms excerpt of a simulated 4 s run, chosen to contain a true pair. Solid line: a true pair accepted. Dashed line: two unrelated flashes accepted by chance.
widget.IbdCoincidence.rocView: Fraction of true pairs kept against the rate of chance pairs, as the window is changed, with the current window marked
widget.IbdCoincidence.rocCap: Each point on the curve is one window width.
widget.IbdCoincidence.cut: Energy cut (prompt 1 to 8 MeV, delayed 1.9 to 2.5 MeV)
widget.IbdCoincidence.note: Simulated, not real data: 1 kHz of single flashes and 20 true pairs per second (far more than a real reactor gives, so the statistics are visible). The second flash of a true pair comes after a delay drawn from an exponential with mean 200 µs. Chance pairs follow R_prompt · R_delayed · Δt, so they shrink in proportion to the window; the signal kept follows 1 − exp(−Δt / 200 µs).
widget.DbdSpectrum.title: Double-beta decay: finding the peak
widget.DbdSpectrum.view: Simulated energy spectrum on a logarithmic scale: a broad continuum from two-neutrino decay and a narrow peak at the end point from neutrinoless decay
widget.DbdSpectrum.cap: Schematic, xenon-136 with Q = {q} MeV. Dashed: continuum alone; solid: continuum plus peak, both blurred by the detector resolution.
widget.DbdSpectrum.visible: The peak stands above the continuum tail inside the window.
widget.DbdSpectrum.swamped: The continuum tail is larger than the peak inside the window: the peak is buried.
widget.DbdSpectrum.note: Schematic. The continuum uses the approximate shape f(K) ∝ K (Q − K)⁵ (1 + 2K + 4K²/3 + K³/3 + K⁴/30), with K and Q in units of the electron mass; the peak is a Gaussian at Q. Both are normalised per unit of total events, and the window is Q ± FWHM. No real half-lives are drawn, and the background from radioactivity is left out.
widget.RotationCurve.title: Rotation curve: with and without a halo
widget.RotationCurve.view: Orbital speed against distance from the galaxy centre: visible disc alone, dark halo alone, and the total
widget.RotationCurve.cap: Model, not data. Dashed: disc alone; dotted: halo alone; solid: total. Dots mark 10 and 25 kpc.
widget.RotationCurve.mratio: Halo mass / disc mass within 25 kpc
widget.RotationCurve.noHalo: No halo: the speed falls with distance and the outer stars would fly off the model.
widget.RotationCurve.falls: The curve falls with distance: the halo is too weak to hold it flat.
widget.RotationCurve.flatMsg: With the halo the curve stays flat, as observed in real galaxies.
widget.RotationCurve.note: Disc: exponential, with the enclosed mass M(r) = M_d [1 − e^(−r/a)(1 + r/a)] (spherical approximation) and v² = G M(r) / r. Halo: pseudo-isothermal with core radius 5 kpc, v_h² = v_flat² [1 − (r_c/r) arctan(r/r_c)]. Total v² = v_disc² + v_halo². Round numbers, for the idea only.
widget.ErNrClassifier.title: Nuclear or electron recoil? Place the cut
widget.ErNrClassifier.view: Simulated events: log of the ratio of the two signals against the first signal. {k} of {n} nuclear recoils and {l} of {m} electron recoils lie below the cut line
widget.ErNrClassifier.cap: Filled markers lie below the cut line and are accepted as nuclear recoils; open markers are rejected. Dashed lines: centre of each band.
widget.ErNrClassifier.sentence: Leakage {leak}, acceptance {acc}. Lowering the line cuts the background and the signal together.
widget.ErNrClassifier.note: Simulated: 60 electron recoils and 60 nuclear recoils, two Gaussian bands, shapes qualitative. Real experiments choose the line from calibration data, often to keep about half of the nuclear recoils while letting through well under one electron recoil in a hundred.
